If a natural person was physically present in the UAE for 183 days or more in the relevant continuous 12-month period, they are considered a UAE Tax Resident for such a 12-month period. It does not matter what activity, if any, is undertaken by the natural person during those 183 days.

The term “day” means a calendar day, and the term “month” means a calendar month for the purposes of meeting the physical presence test. Being physically present refers to being within the state borders of the UAE.

For the purposes of calculating whether the 183-day threshold has been met, any day or any part of a day, however brief, that a natural person was present in the UAE will be counted as a full day. The days do not need to be consecutive. If any of the days the natural person spent in the UAE were due to exceptional circumstances, these may be disregarded for the purposes of meeting the threshold. For more information about exceptional circumstances, see Section 5.2.3 .
Example 12: Days spent in the UAE
In 2025, Harry spends the following days in the UAE:
Days in the UAE Travel to the UAE Travel from the UAE (inclusive of travel days)
3 January 6 March 63
8 June 9 August 63
23 August 6 September 15
28 September 11 November 45
Total 186
As any “part of day” is included when considering the “physically present test”, Harry should include the days of travel to and from the UAE when calculating his days of presence in the UAE.
As a result, in 2025, Harry has spent 186 days in the UAE. He can, therefore, be considered a UAE Tax Resident for the 12-month period from January to December 2025.

If a natural person was physically present in the UAE for fewer than 183 days in the relevant continuous 12-month period, they may still be considered a UAE Tax Resident if they were present in the UAE for at least 90 days and also meet both of the following conditions:
they have a legal right to reside in the UAE by virtue of being a national of the UAE or another GCC Member State, or holding a valid Residence Permit in the UAE, and
they also have a “Permanent Place of Residence” in the UAE or carry on employment or a Business in the UAE.
The meaning and determination of what constitutes a “day” for the purposes of the 90- day test is the same as in the 183-day test.

A Permanent Place of Residence means a furnished house, apartment, room or other form of dwelling, which a natural person has arranged to have made continuously available to them. This means that a Permanent Place of Residence does not need to be owned by the natural person to meet this test, but can be rented or otherwise occupied by the natural person as a dwelling, provided it is available to them at all times continuously and on a regular basis, with some degree of permanency and stability, based on a right of occupation.

A place will not be considered a Permanent Place of Residence if it is occupied by the natural person just occasionally or temporarily for the purposes of a stay which is for a short duration, for example, for the purposes of travel for business, leisure or education.

There is a distinction between a Permanent Place of Residence for the purposes of Article 4(3) of Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022 and a usual or primary place of residence for the purposes of its Article 4(1) of Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022. A usual or primary place of residence refers to the country where a natural person normally resides (see Section 5.2.4.1 ), whereas a Permanent Place of Residence refers to a form of dwelling that is continuously available to the natural person, regardless of whether they habitually reside there.
Example 13: 90+ days physically present and Permanent Place of Residence

During 2024, Fatima spent 95 days staying in a one-bedroom apartment in Dubai, UAE, which her sister, Nadia, owns but does not occupy. Nadia has given Fatima full access to the apartment, so Fatima can use it whenever she stays in the city. Fatima is a foreign national who holds a long-term UAE Residence Permit.
Fatima should be considered a UAE Tax Resident for the 12-month period from January to December 2024 because:
she has been physically present in the UAE for over 90 days in 2024, and
she has the legal right to reside in the UAE because she holds a UAE Residence Permit, and
she has a Permanent Place of Residence in the UAE given her ability to continuously access and stay in Nadia's apartment at any given time and for any duration.
Nadia's apartment still counts as a Permanent Place of Residence for Fatima, even though Fatima does not own it and she does not pay Nadia any rent for occupying the apartment.
Example 14: 90+ days physically present and no Permanent Place of Residence

Sulaiman, a non-UAE and non-GCC citizen, enjoys spending time in the UAE. During the 12 months of calendar year 2024, he spent 100 days in the UAE, entering the country under tourist visas. While in the UAE, Sulaiman stayed in a number of different hotels he booked online and he spent most of his time in the UAE doing leisure activities such as shopping and sightseeing. He does not conduct any Business in the UAE, nor carry out any employment in the UAE.
Sulaiman should not be considered a UAE Tax Resident for the 12 months ended 31 December 2024 because even though he has spent over 90 days in the relevant 12-month period in the UAE:
he does not have a legal right to permanently reside in the UAE and has always entered the UAE as a tourist, and
he does not have a Permanent Place of Residence in the UAE.
He also did not carry on employment or Business in the UAE, or hold a valid Residence Permit.

The hotels where Sulaiman has stayed do not count as a Permanent Place of Residence in the UAE for him as he stayed there only temporarily for leisure purposes. The hotel rooms were not continuously made available to him, he had to check the availability and make a booking each time prior to his arrival.
A natural person will be considered to be carrying on employment in the UAE, if:

they are party to a contract with an employer, which is incorporated or otherwise formed or recognised in the UAE, under which they serve the employer under the employer’s administration or supervision for a promised remuneration by the employer,
they are in a continuing relationship where all or substantially all of their income for their labour performed in the UAE is derived from one party, and
it is not an engagement on a voluntary role.
Employment status does not consider the nature of the employment contract, which can be limited or unlimited, on a full-time or part-time basis.

Business is defined as an activity conducted regularly, on an ongoing and independent basis by any Person, such as industrial, commercial, agricultural, professional, vocational, service or excavation activities or anything related to the use of tangible or intangible properties.
Business should be interpreted broadly to include any activity such as the development, sale, production, manufacturing, exploitation, marketing or distribution of tangible and intangible properties.

The term “vocational” is to be interpreted as a skilled craft or trade, and “professional” is an occupation in which skill is applied to the affairs of others to meet their needs. Common examples of vocational and professional activities include accountancy, craftsmanship, consulting, teaching, architecture, medical and legal services.

Business can mean the carrying out of any economic activity, whether continuous or for a set period of time, by any Person; it does not necessarily need to generate a profit. Although a Business is typically carried on continuously and there is repetition of commercial activity, the definition allows for a short-term commercial activity to also be considered a Business.
Example 15: 90 days+ and employment in the UAE

Saleh is a GCC national. In the last 12 months, he was employed by Company O, a UAE incorporated company, to travel to different destinations in the UAE and promote their products. His employment lasted three months and he spent a total of 100 days in the UAE. Saleh held a UAE work visa during this time.

While in the UAE, Saleh stayed in various hotel rooms booked and paid for by Company O. As such, he did not have a Permanent Place of Residence in the UAE. Still, Saleh was a UAE Tax Resident for the 12-month period because:
he was physically present in the UAE for over 90 days in the year, and
he has the legal right to reside in the UAE because he is a GCC national, and
he had employment in the UAE by virtue of his employment contract with a company incorporated in the UAE.
Even though Saleh is considered a Tax Resident in the UAE, he is not a Resident Person for Corporate Tax purposes because he does not conduct any Business in the UAE.

blocks.title: Exceptional circumstances leading to a physical presence

blocks.text: There are occasions in which natural persons will be physically present in the UAE for reasons beyond their control. An exceptional circumstance is an event occurring while the natural person is already in the UAE, which prevents them from leaving the UAE as originally planned. The exceptional circumstance must be an event beyond the natural person's control that they could not reasonably have predicted or prevented.
Examples of exceptional circumstances may include, but are not limited to:
local or national emergencies, for example, natural disasters, closing of borders, war or civil unrest,
personal emergencies, for example, a sudden or critical illness or injury to the natural person.

As a result, a natural person may inadvertently be a UAE Tax Resident. When calculating the number of days that a natural person has spent in the UAE, the days they stayed in the UAE due to exceptional circumstances shall be disregarded.
Example 16: Exceptional circumstances
Nicholas spent 180 days in the UAE during 2025. He visited the UAE on tourist visas and has no employment or business connections to the UAE.

On the day before he was due to fly back to his home country, Nicholas suddenly fell critically ill. He was required to spend an additional week in the UAE so that he th could have emergency surgery. He flew home on his 187 day in the UAE.

Normally, the fact that Nicholas spent over 183 days in the UAE would result in him being considered a Tax Resident in the UAE. However, as his extended stay was the result of a medical emergency that he could not control and could not have reasonably predicted or prevented, the additional days he spent in the UAE should be excluded when calculating his total number of days in the UAE.

This means that, despite being physically present in the UAE for over 183 days, Nicholas may not necessarily be considered a Tax Resident for the relevant 12- month period under the days count test as he has no employment or other significant connections to the UAE.
Example 17: Non-exceptional circumstances
Sam spent 175 days in the UAE during 2024. He is a non-UAE and non-GCC national with a UAE tourist visa, with no permanent home in the UAE.
Instead of flying home, Sam decided to stay in the UAE for a few additional days in order to have an elective medical procedure in a hospital in Dubai.

As a result of his extended stay, Sam spent a total of 190 days in the UAE during 2024. As he made the conscious decision to schedule the elective medical procedure knowing it would require recovery time in the UAE, the additional days spent in the UAE beyond 180 days were within Sam’s control and will not be classed as exceptional circumstances.
Therefore, Sam is considered to be UAE Tax Resident under the physical presence test.

blocks.title: Usual or primary place of residence and centre of financial and personal interests test

blocks.text: A natural person will be considered a Tax Resident in the UAE if both their usual or primary place of residence and the centre of their financial and personal interests are in the UAE. Both of these conditions must be simultaneously satisfied in order for a natural person to be considered a UAE Tax Resident.

blocks.title: Usual or primary place of residence

blocks.text: A “usual or primary place of residence” refers to the country where a natural person habitually or normally lives as a part of their settled routine and where they spend most of their time as compared to any other place.

This is the country in which a natural person is customarily or usually present, which depends on the frequency, duration and regularity of stays that are part of a person's life over a sufficient length of time.

The concept of “usual or primary place of residence” is distinct from a “Permanent Place of Residence” (or permanent home). A usual or primary place of residence refers to the country where a natural person normally resides, whereas a Permanent Place of Residence refers to a form of dwelling that is continuously available to the natural person, regardless of whether they habitually reside there.

blocks.title: Centre of their financial and personal interests

blocks.text: The “centre of financial and personal interests” condition considers factors such as the place of employment, place of business, and where the financial and other investments are located and managed. It also considers other factors such as family and social connections, memberships of clubs and associations and any cultural and other activities the natural person takes part in.

Having one’s centre of financial and personal interests in the UAE does not mean that the natural person cannot have interests outside the UAE. However, the UAE must be the place where these interests are the closest or of the greatest significance to the natural person.

It is not only the number of connections but also the depths and importance of those connections that is considered. For example, the location of close family members or a business in the UAE has a more significant weight than holding a membership of a sports club in another country.
Example 18: Usual or primary place of residence and centre of financial and personal interests’ criteria

Laila is a UAE national, who owns an apartment in Sharjah, UAE. However, she spends most of her time in Country P, where she has lived with her husband and children in a house owned by her parents for the past 10 years. Laila has a full-time job in Country P as a teacher and she is an integral part of the local community.

Every year, Laila spends a few weeks outside of Country P when she travels to the UAE to see her extended family and friends, during which time she stays in her apartment in Sharjah. She intends to use the apartment as her main home at some point in the future. In the last 12 months, she spent a total of 30 days in the UAE.

Based on these facts, Laila’s usual or primary place of residence is in Country P because this is where she habitually lives and spends more time as compared to the UAE and any other country. The fact that her employment, close family members and social ties are also all in Country P indicates that her centre of financial and personal interests is also in Country P. Therefore, for the last 12 months, based on the “usual or primary place of residence and centre of financial and personal interests” test, Laila is not considered a UAE Tax Resident.
Example 19: Usual or primary place of residence’s criteria

Caleb was born in Country Q but has moved to the UAE, where he is a full-time university student. He lives in an apartment in the UAE, which he rents on an annual basis, and he travels back to Country Q for one month each summer.

The UAE is the country where Caleb normally lives and he spends more time in the UAE than in Country Q or any other country. Based on these facts, Caleb has his usual or primary place of residence in the UAE.
Example 20: Centre of financial and personal interests’ criteria
Aria is a citizen of Country R. Five years ago, Aria was offered the opportunity to relocate to the UAE with her husband and son. She left her job in Country R and

now works full-time in the UAE. She and her husband sold their apartment in Country R and have purchased a villa in the UAE close to their son’s school, where they normally reside. She is a member of a tennis club and volunteers for a local charity every weekend. Her parents still live in Country R and she keeps a bank account there, which she uses occasionally when she visits.

Based on these facts, the UAE is the place where Aria’s centre of financial and personal interests is closest and of greatest significance to her. Despite her still having extended family in Country R, the UAE is the place where her close family members, her husband and son, are located. It is also the place where her full-time job/main source of income and only property are located. Her social and other connections are closer to the UAE than in Country R.

blocks.title: Tax residency under Double Taxation Agreements

blocks.text: Each DTA has its own rules and criteria for determining when juridical and natural persons are considered to be tax resident in the countries which are party to the DTA. This may differ from the criteria for determining who is a UAE Tax Resident under domestic law, or a Resident Person under the Corporate Tax Law. Therefore, each scenario should be considered on a case-by-case basis and in light of the wording of the specific DTA.

A DTA that is in force in the UAE, takes precedence over the provisions of any domestic law, including the Corporate Tax Law and Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022. Therefore, meeting the definition of a Resident Person under the Corporate Tax Law does not automatically mean that a Resident Person will be considered a tax resident in the UAE for the purposes of a DTA.

A key feature of DTAs are the rules that determine in which country the juridical person is tax resident. Under an applicable DTA, tax residence may be assigned to the UAE or to another jurisdiction depending on the facts and circumstances and the residence criteria of the relevant agreement (“treaty resident”). The list of countries with which the UAE has signed a DTA can be found on the Ministry of Finance website.

blocks.title: Juridical persons that are tax resident under Double Taxation Agreements

blocks.text: Residency is defined in each DTA in a specific manner. In general, the tax residency test in a DTA typically requires a juridical person seeking to apply the DTA to either be liable to tax, have a legal connection (for example, incorporation), or economic connection (for example, effective management or substantial presence), or a combination thereof, in the relevant country.

If a juridical person is considered to be a tax resident in the UAE under the applicable DTA, it is eligible to apply for a Tax Residency Certificate in the UAE in order to obtain the benefits of the applicable DTA, if required.

blocks.title: Tax residence of Government Entities under Double Taxation Agreements

blocks.text: Government Entities are automatically considered Exempt Persons for Corporate Tax purposes. Additionally, Government Controlled Entities are Exempt Persons in relation to income from their Mandated Activities.

In the context of DTAs, Government Entities and Government Controlled Entities are generally considered as UAE tax resident and should accordingly be eligible to avail benefits under the DTAs, wherever relevant. However, if the relevant DTA defines Government for the purposes of the DTA, this shall prevail.

blocks.title: Tax residence of Exempt Persons under Double Taxation Agreements

blocks.text: If an Exempt Person is considered a tax resident under the provisions of the DTA, it can benefit from its provisions. Some DTAs have specific rules for juridical persons that are commonly exempt from Corporate Tax such as Government Entities, public benefit entities and pension funds. Where a DTA’s criteria is based on being liable to tax, Exempt Persons will be able to benefit from its provisions, as they are all considered liable to tax in the UAE.

blocks.title: Double Taxation Agreements tie-breaker rules for juridical persons

blocks.text: DTAs adopt various approaches to solve dual residence situations for juridical persons. These are generally summarised as follows:
the place of effective management criteria,
the Mutual Agreement Procedure, and
other criteria, such as where the head office is located or where the juridical person is incorporated.

Following the pre-2017 OECD Model Tax Convention, a company that has dual-residency status is considered tax resident for tax purposes in the country in which its place of effective management and control is situated.

The OECD Commentary defines place of effective management as the place where the key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the entity’s business as a whole are in substance made, and makes the point that whilst an entity may have multiple places of management, it can only have one place of effective management at any one point in time.
Example 21: Dual residence of juridical person incorporated in one country and effectively managed and controlled in another country

Company S is a limited liability company incorporated in Country S. However, all of the company’s board meetings take place in the UAE and all key management and commercial decisions are made in the UAE.

Under Country S’s domestic law, Company S is tax resident in Country S due to being incorporated in Country S. However, under UAE domestic law, Company S is considered to be tax resident in the UAE on the basis that it is effectively managed and controlled in the UAE.

As a result, Company S is tax resident in both the UAE and in Country S. However, in instances where a juridical person is tax resident in both countries, the applicable DTA between Country S and the UAE provides for a tie-breaker to allocate tax residency to the country in which a juridical person is effectively managed and controlled.
This means that Company S will only be tax resident in the UAE because the company is effectively managed and controlled in the UAE.

Following the 2017 OECD Model Tax Convention, many DTAs consider the Mutual Agreement Procedure (“MAP”) in instances of dual residence. The MAP is a mechanism through which the competent authorities of the countries involved endeavour to resolve differences or difficulties on the interpretation or application of the DTA on a mutually agreed basis, including cases where the residency status is unclear.

blocks.title: Other criteria to solve dual residence situations

blocks.text: Many DTAs entered into by the UAE rely on other criteria to solve dual residence situations such as the place of incorporation or the place where the head office is located.

blocks.title: Natural persons that are tax resident under Double Taxation Agreements

blocks.text: As discussed, the concept of a natural person being a Resident Person for Corporate Tax purposes is separate to the concept of the natural person’s tax residency status.
A natural person will be considered a UAE tax resident for DTA purposes if he or she meets the conditions set out in the applicable DTA.

The UAE has an extensive DTA network, which aims to avoid a situation of double taxation by defining the taxing rights of each country or granting relief from double taxation. These DTAs have their own rules and criteria for determining when natural persons are considered tax resident in the countries which are party to the DTA.

As each DTA has its own tax residency rules, it is important to confirm the definition and criteria of a tax resident under the relevant DTA (generally, set out in the provision equivalent to Article 4 of the OECD’s Model Tax Convention).

In general, the residency criteria in a DTA typically requires an individual seeking to apply the DTA to either be liable to tax, to have the relevant citizenship or nationality, to have physical presence in the relevant country, or be domiciled or resident there.

If the criteria in a DTA includes a reference to being “resident under the laws of the United Arab Emirates”, the requirement to be Tax Resident as per Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022 is the relevant criteria (see Section 5 ).

blocks.title: Double Taxation Agreement tie-breaker rules for natural persons

blocks.text: Where a natural person satisfies the criteria to be considered tax resident in both the UAE and in another jurisdiction under the relevant DTA, the tie-breaker rules in the DTA would allocate the residence of the natural person to either the UAE or to the other country.
The tie-breaker rules typically consider:
In which country is the natural person’s permanent home located?
If the natural person has a permanent home in both countries, where is the natural person’s “centre of vital interests”?

If the natural person does not have a permanent home in either country, or if the location of the natural person’s centre of vital interests cannot be determined, where is the natural person’s “habitual abode”?
If the natural person has their habitual abode in both jurisdictions or in neither of them, of which jurisdiction is the natural person a “national”?

Where the tie-breaker rules do not resolve the dual residency status of the natural person, the competent authorities under the relevant DTA may consult with each other and agree the natural person’s tax residency status. Determining the tax residency for a natural person is heavily dependent on facts and circumstances for each specific case.

To determine tax residence, a permanent home means a house, apartment, furnished room or other form of dwelling, which the natural person has arranged to have made continuously available to them. A permanent home does not need to be owned by the natural person but can be rented or otherwise occupied by the natural person, provided it is available to them at all times continuously. The natural person also needs to regularly occupy the home, with some degree of permanency and stability, based on a right of occupation.
A permanent home is not a place occupied by the natural person occasionally or temporarily, for example, for the purposes of travel for business, leisure or education.

This test applies to the period of time in which the natural person’s residency position affects their tax liability. For example, if a natural person moves to a new country and changes their permanent residence part-way through a Financial Year, the original country would treat the natural person as a resident until the date of the move, after which, the new country would treat the natural person as a tax resident.

If a natural person has two places that could be considered as home at any point in time, the question arises as to which one, if any, is “permanent”. This is often where the natural person arranges and retains a home for permanent use, as opposed to staying at a particular place for a short duration. The accommodation should be continuously available at all times to pass the permanent home test.

Centre of vital interests is the country with which a natural person’s personal and economic relations are the closest. This requires a holistic assessment of the natural person's family and social relations, their occupation and place of business, any political and cultural activities and the place from which they administer their property.

Both the number as well as the depth and importance of the natural person’s connections should be considered in determining where the centre of vital interests is located. For example, the location of family members in one jurisdiction may be a more decisive factor than the membership of various sports and social clubs in another country.
A natural person cannot have more than one centre of vital interests but if that centre cannot be determined in practice, the next test (“habitual abode”) should be applied.

If the counting of days in a particular period does not determine where the natural person is resident, then a longer period of time may be considered in order to determine where the natural person habitually spends their time.
To determine where the individual has a habitual abode, factors such as the frequency of the person’s visits, as well as the length and purpose of their stay is considered.

If a natural person habitually spends equal amounts of time between two countries, and the connection does not prevail in relation to one of the countries, then the final test (“nationality”) is applied.
Finally, the natural person should be considered resident in the country of which they are a national.
Where they are a national of both countries or neither of them, the cross-border tax dispute shall be decided by the two contracting states through a MAP.

blocks.title: Non-resident under the Double Taxation Agreement

blocks.text: Where the natural person is considered resident in a foreign country covered by a DTA between the UAE and that foreign country, the provisions of the applicable DTA has an impact on his or her tax residency status.

This may depend on the nature of the income derived in the UAE by the natural person. Any income that falls under the “Business Profits” article of the relevant DTA (generally, set out in the provision equivalent to Article 7 of the OECD Model Tax Convention) would generally remain taxable in the UAE if the non-resident natural person has a Permanent Establishment in the UAE. In this case, the natural person is subject to Corporate Tax on the income attributable to the Permanent Establishment in the UAE.

Generally, the application of the DTA is only relevant where the total Turnover from the Businesses or Business Activities conducted in the UAE exceeds AED 1 million in a Gregorian calendar year, which is the triggering criteria for a natural person to be subject to Corporate Tax.

Where a non-resident natural person does not conduct a Business or Business Activity in the UAE, he or she may be subject to Corporate Tax on State Sourced Income. However, this is currently via a Withholding Tax rate of 0%.
A Tax Residency Certificate is a certificate issued by the FTA proving that the Person is a Tax Resident in the UAE.
A Tax Residency Certificate can be obtained for DTA purposes and for purposes other than the application of a DTA.
The relevant criteria for obtaining a Tax Residency Certificate and the relevant procedure are further detailed below.

blocks.title: Periods covered by the Tax Residency Certificate

blocks.text: Applicants must include which Tax Period or other 12-month period to be covered by the Tax Residency Certificate, depending on the specific situation. If a Tax Period is selected, it can only be the current Tax Period or a prior Tax Period.
For juridical persons, the Tax Period is the Financial Year. Generally, this is the 12- month period for which the Taxable Person prepares Financial Statements.
For natural persons, the Tax Period is the Gregorian calendar year.
Where a Tax Residency Certificate is required for the current period, the application will only be considered by the FTA as follows:

rows: After three (3) months into the period.
As soon as the criteria to be Tax Resident are met.
Government Entities and Government Controlled Entities

blocks.text: A Tax Residency Certificate cannot be obtained for a future period (i.e. for a Tax Period or a 12-month period that has not commenced), as the FTA cannot certify that a Person will continue to be UAE Tax Resident for a future period.
In addition, a Tax Residency Certificate cannot be obtained for a period longer than 12 months.
Newly incorporated companies who have yet to file a Corporate Tax Return must be established for 12 months before being eligible to apply for a Tax Residency Certificate.
As Exempt Persons are considered to be liable to tax, they are, therefore, able to apply for a Tax Residency Certificate.

blocks.title: How to apply for a Tax Residency Certificate

blocks.text: A juridical person or natural person can apply for a Tax Residency Certificate via the FTA's online EmaraTax portal, using their EmaraTax account. The steps are provided below:
Step 1 : Go to the EmaraTax portal. https://eservices.tax.gov.ae/ar-ae/login?returnurl=%2far-ae%2fuser%2fdashboard
Step 2 : Create an account.
You can use a current account on EmaraTax, create a new one, or link the old account related to the previous Tax Certificate portal.
Step 3 : Once logged in, choose “other services”.
Step 4: Select “Tax Residency Certificate”.
Step 5 : Select the Tax Registration Number (“TRN”) for Corporate Tax for the applicant applying for a Tax Residency Certificate.
If there is no Corporate Tax TRN, choose the last option "No TRN". However, if you are obtaining a Tax Residency Certificate for the purposes of a DTA, the other contracting state may require this.
Providing a TRN will reduce the application fees and also entitle the applicant to autofill the details in the application.
Step 6 : Select the type of Tax Residency Certificate requested.
This will either be for the purposes of a DTA or otherwise. For those applying to benefit from a DTA, the other applicable country will need to be selected first.
Step 7 : Complete the remaining fields and upload supporting documentation.
This will include the ability to request printed certificates and request the FTA to attest an international form (see Section 8).
Step 8 : Pay the submission fees (see Section 7.7 ).
Step 9 : Submit the application.
Step 10 : After obtaining FTA’s approval, pay the processing fees (see Section 7.7 ).

Failure to pay the processing fees within 30 business days may result in your application being cancelled. Instead, the applicant would be required to resubmit a new application and repay the submission fee.
Step 11 : Download the certificate.

Once the applicant has paid the processing amount, a download icon will be displayed for the particular request from the Tax Residency Certificate platform, in which the applicant can click and download the digital Tax Residency Certificate.
The Tax Residency Certificate will also be sent to their registered email ID.
If applicant also requested a printed certificate, it will be delivered by courier (Emirates post).

blocks.title: Applying for a Tax Residency Certificate for the purposes of a Double Taxation Agreement

blocks.text: If the FTA is satisfied that the applicant meets the conditions to be considered a Tax Resident in the UAE in accordance with the provisions of the relevant DTA, the FTA will approve the application and issue a Tax Residency Certificate, stating the applicable DTA.
The application must include all necessary information for the FTA to be able to review and issue the Tax Residency Certificate, as further detailed below.
Where the other country requires a specific form to be stamped to avail benefits under a DTA, this service is also available from the FTA (see Section 8 ).

The FTA will only issue a Tax Residency Certificate where it is satisfied that the Person meets the criteria to be a UAE Tax Resident. As a result, the FTA can request supporting evidence and any documentation which it deems necessary for deciding whether to issue a Tax Residency Certificate. The following documentation will typically be required for the application period, where relevant.

Upon submission of the application, the FTA will review the application and, if approved, issue the Tax Residency Certificate for applicants to download. Users can request hard copies of their certificates for an additional fee.

The Tax Residency Certificate is only applicable to the period selected by the applicant. However, the FTA has the authority to withdraw a Tax Residency Certificate if they become aware of incorrect information or a change in facts that prevent the applicant from being a Tax Resident.

The FTA takes, in general, 10 business days to respond from the date the completed application was received. A response will be in the form of approval, rejection or request for further information. If there is a request for further information, the applicant has 30 business days to respond, with an option to request an extension through resubmission. This is to allow the applicant to obtain all the relevant documents and information in sufficient time (for example, to renew a Licence or passport).

If the applicant requests hard copies of the certificate, the FTA will take 5 business days to respond from the date the certificate fee payment is completed. The FTA will only deliver to addresses in the UAE. The cost of this service is included within the fee for requesting a hard copy of the certificate.

The issuance of a Tax Residency Certificate is subject to certain fees as determined by Cabinet Decision No. 65 of 2020. The submission fee to obtain a Tax Residency Certificate is AED 50 and non-refundable. Once approved, the processing fee is as follows:

Some jurisdictions require Persons applying to avail benefits under a DTA to provide an authorised or signed document to show that they are a Tax Resident of a particular jurisdiction with which an applicable DTA exists. Generally, jurisdictions should accept a Tax Residency Certificate issued by the FTA as evidence of a Person’s tax residency in the UAE. However, some jurisdictions provide their own Tax Residency Certificate forms which they require to be stamped by the tax authority in the country where a Person claims to be a tax resident.

The FTA can, upon request, stamp forms provided by other jurisdictions. The form should be filled in and duly signed and stamped by the applicant and must cover the same 12-month period and jurisdiction as the applicant’s relevant Tax Residency Certificate. In cases of a juridical person, a stamp is also required by the authorised signatory.

The original form provided by the other jurisdiction should be in English or Arabic. If not, the form should be translated into either English or Arabic. The translation must be approved in accordance with the law regulating translation in the UAE.

In order to have their form signed and stamped, the applicant must send the form by courier service to the FTA. The cost for the service of international form stamping is included in the Tax Residency Certificate processing fee. However, the applicant will bear fees for sending and returning the documents.

If the applicant does not purchase a return courier service, the applicant will be required to collect the documents and form physically from the relevant FTA office. These documents will only be retained by the FTA for six months from the date of notifying the applicant.
The FTA can also electronically send the signed and stamped form to the applicant, upon request, for no additional fee.

FTA takes, in general, 10 business days to respond from the date the completed form is received and the processing fee of the relevant Tax Residency Certificate has been paid. A response will be in the form of sending the international form via the applicant’s pre-paid return courier service or a notification that the documents are ready to be collected.
Applicants also have the option to submit any specific forms online as a scanned copy to be signed with an FTA ink signature, provided it is recognised and accepted by the other country.

The specified form can be attached alongside the application in Tax Residency Certificate portal. It will be returned through the application with the required signature. The form should be filled by the taxpayer and it should match the application in the system in terms of the Financial Year of the certificate.
